docs.title: Home
docs.text:
chemhelper solves the problems that fill the first semester of general chemistry: molar mass, percent composition, converting between grams, moles and molarity, and the ideal gas law. Every solver has a twin whose name ends in _steps that prints the solution the way you would write it on a whiteboard.

It was written by a chemistry tutor, for tutoring. Check a student's answer in a second, show exactly where it came from, and spend the rest of the session on understanding.

Just the answerThe worked solutionA whole problem 
>>> from chemhelper import compounds
>>> compounds.mass('Ca(OH)2')
74.1

>>> from chemhelper import compounds
>>> compounds.mass_steps('Ca(OH)2')
Ca(OH)2
Ca: 40.08
O: 2 x 16.0 = 32.0
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016

Mass Ca(OH)2 = 40.08 + 32.0 + 2.016 = 74.1

How many grams of NaCl do you need for 2 L of a 0.5 M solution?

>>> from chemhelper import conversions
>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps(0.5, 2, 'NaCl')
0.5 moles/L x 2 L = 1 moles
NaCl
Na: 22.99
Cl: 35.45

Mass NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44
1 moles x 58.44 grams/mole = 58.44 grams

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Shows its work

    Every solver has a _steps twin. The printed solution includes units and each intermediate value.

  • Reads like chemistry

    Formulas are written the way they appear in a textbook, parentheses and all. Arguments are named after the quantities.

  • Tells you what went wrong

    A typo in a formula or a missing value raises an error that names the problem, not a cryptic traceback.

  • Tested examples

    Every example on this site is run against the real package before the site is published.

docs.title: Cookbook
docs.text:
Short recipes for single tasks. Each one stands alone, given these imports:

>>> from chemhelper import elements, compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

docs.title: Molar masses for a list of compounds
docs.text:
>>> formulas = ['H2O', 'CO2', 'NaCl', 'C6H12O6', 'Ca(OH)2']
>>> {f: compounds.mass(f) for f in formulas}
{'H2O': 18.02, 'CO2': 44.01, 'NaCl': 58.44, 'C6H12O6': 180.16, 'Ca(OH)2': 74.1}

As a table, sorted from heaviest to lightest:

>>> import pandas as pd
>>> table = pd.Series({f: compounds.mass(f) for f in formulas}, name='g/mol')
>>> table.sort_values(ascending=False)
C6H12O6    180.16
Ca(OH)2     74.10
NaCl        58.44
CO2         44.01
H2O         18.02
Name: g/mol, dtype: float64

docs.title: Count the atoms in a formula
docs.text:
>>> counts = compounds.parse_formula('Ca3(PO4)2')
>>> dict(counts)
{'Ca': 3, 'P': 2, 'O': 8}
>>> sum(counts.values())
13

docs.title: Check that a formula is valid
docs.text:
>>> def is_valid(formula):
...     try:
...         compounds.parse_formula(formula)
...         return True
...     except ValueError:
...         return False
>>> [is_valid(f) for f in ['H2O', 'h2o', 'Ca(OH)2', 'Ca(OH2']]
[True, False, True, False]

docs.title: Molar mass of a hydrate
docs.text:
Write the water of hydration in parentheses. Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O:

>>> compounds.mass('CuSO4(H2O)5')
249.7

docs.title: Percent water in a hydrate
docs.text:
Divide the mass of the water by the mass of the whole hydrate:

>>> round(5 * compounds.mass('H2O') / compounds.mass('CuSO4(H2O)5') * 100, 2)
36.08

docs.title: Compare an element's share across compounds
docs.text:
Which iron ore is richest in iron?

>>> for ore in ['Fe2O3', 'Fe3O4', 'FeCO3', 'FeS2']:
...     print(ore, float(compounds.percent_composition(ore)['Fe']))
Fe2O3 69.944
Fe3O4 72.36
FeCO3 48.205
FeS2 46.546

docs.title: Check an empirical formula against percent composition
docs.text:
A compound is 40.0 % C, 6.7 % H and 53.3 % O. Is CH₂O a possible empirical formula?

>>> compounds.percent_composition('CH2O')
C          39.999
H           6.714
O          53.287
Total:    100.000
Name: CH2O, dtype: float64

The percentages match. Glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, has the same empirical formula and so the same percent composition:

>>> compounds.percent_composition('C6H12O6')
C          39.999
H           6.714
O          53.287
Total:    100.000
Name: C6H12O6, dtype: float64

docs.title: Find the molecular formula from a molar mass
docs.text:
The empirical formula is CH₂O and the molar mass is about 180 g/mol.

>>> round(180 / compounds.mass('CH2O'))
6

The molecular formula is six empirical units: C₆H₁₂O₆.

docs.title: Number of molecules in a sample
docs.text:
Multiply moles by Avogadro's number. chemhelper does not define the constant, so write it in:

>>> AVOGADRO = 6.022e23
>>> moles = conversions.grams_to_moles(18.02, 'H2O')
>>> moles * AVOGADRO
6.022e+23

docs.title: Mass of a single molecule, in grams
docs.text:
>>> '{:.3e}'.format(compounds.mass('H2O') / 6.022e23)
'2.992e-23'

docs.title: Grams of an element in a sample of a compound
docs.text:
How many grams of iron are in 250 g of Fe₂O₃?

>>> fraction = float(compounds.percent_composition('Fe2O3')['Fe']) / 100
>>> round(250 * fraction, 1)
174.9

docs.title: Grams of product from grams of reactant
docs.text:
N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃. How many grams of ammonia form from 56.0 g of N₂?

>>> moles_n2 = conversions.grams_to_moles(56.0, 'N2')
>>> moles_nh3 = moles_n2 * 2 / 1
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(moles_nh3, 'NH3')
68.12

The 2 / 1 is the mole ratio of NH₃ to N₂ from the balanced equation.

docs.title: Find the limiting reagent
docs.text:
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. You have 10.0 g of H₂ and 64.0 g of O₂.

Divide each reactant's moles by its coefficient. The smallest result is the limiting reagent.

>>> h2 = conversions.grams_to_moles(10.0, 'H2') / 2
>>> o2 = conversions.grams_to_moles(64.0, 'O2') / 1
>>> h2, o2
(2.475, 2.0)
>>> 'H2' if h2 < o2 else 'O2'
'O2'

Water formed, from the limiting reagent:

>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(o2 * 2, 'H2O')
72.08

docs.title: Percent yield
docs.text:
The theoretical yield is 72.08 g and you collected 61.3 g.

>>> round(61.3 / 72.08 * 100, 1)
85.0

docs.title: Molarity from milliliters
docs.text:
>>> conversions.molarity(250 / 1000, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
1.0

docs.title: Grams needed for a list of concentrations
docs.text:
>>> for M in [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]:
...     print(M, 'M:', conversions.molarity_to_grams(M, 0.500, 'NaCl'), 'g')
0.1 M: 2.92 g
0.25 M: 7.3 g
0.5 M: 14.61 g
1.0 M: 29.22 g

docs.title: Dilution
docs.text:
25.0 mL of 6.0 M acid diluted to 500 mL.

>>> round(conversions.molarity(0.500, moles=conversions.molarity_to_moles(6.0, 0.0250)), 3)
0.3

docs.title: Concentration in grams per liter
docs.text:
>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.15, 1, 'NaCl')
8.77

docs.title: Molar volume at a given temperature and pressure
docs.text:
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, P=1, T=25, Tunits='C')
24.48

docs.title: Density of a gas
docs.text:
Density is the mass of one mole divided by the volume of one mole.

>>> molar_volume = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, P=1, T=25, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
>>> round(compounds.mass('CO2') / molar_volume, 3)
1.798

That is in grams per liter.

docs.title: Pressure in other units
docs.text:
>>> p = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', n=0.5, V=10, T=300)
>>> {'atm': p, 'torr': round(p * 760, 1), 'kPa': round(p * 101.325, 1)}
{'atm': 1.23, 'torr': 934.8, 'kPa': 124.6}

docs.title: Volume across a range of temperatures
docs.text:
>>> for celsius in [0, 25, 50, 100]:
...     print(celsius, 'C:', ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, P=1, T=celsius, Tunits='C'), 'L')
0 C: 22.43 L
25 C: 24.48 L
50 C: 26.53 L
100 C: 30.64 L

docs.title: Capture a worked solution as a string
docs.text:
_steps functions print. This helper returns what any of them would have printed:

>>> import contextlib, io
>>> def solution_text(steps_function, *args, **kwargs):
...     buffer = io.StringIO()
...     with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
...         steps_function(*args, **kwargs)
...     return buffer.getvalue()
>>> text = solution_text(compounds.mass_steps, 'NaCl')
>>> print(text)
NaCl
Na: 22.99
Cl: 35.45

Mass NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44

docs.title: Save a worked solution to a file
docs.text:
with open('solution.txt', 'w') as f:
    f.write(solution_text(conversions.molarity_steps, 0.25, mass=10, chemical='NaOH'))

docs.title: Writing formulas
docs.text:
Every function that takes a compound takes it as a formula string such as 'H2O'. This page describes exactly what the parser accepts.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
1. Element symbols are case-sensitive. A symbol is one capital letter, optionally followed by one lowercase letter: C, Co, Ca, Cl.
  2. A number after a symbol is its count. No number means one: H2O is two hydrogens and one oxygen.
  3. Groups go in parentheses or square brackets, followed by an optional count: Ca(OH)2, [Fe(CN)6].
  4. Groups can be nested to any depth: K4[Fe(CN)6].
  5. An element may appear more than once. Its counts are added together: CH3COOH is C₂H₄O₂.
  6. Spaces are ignored.

Only elements 1 to 92 (H to U) are known. See the periodic table.

docs.title: Examples that work
docs.text: You write Meaning Counted as 'H2O' water H 2, O 1 'NaCl' sodium chloride Na 1, Cl 1 'C6H12O6' glucose C 6, H 12, O 6 'Ca(OH)2' calcium hydroxide Ca 1, O 2, H 2 'Al2(SO4)3' aluminum sulfate Al 2, S 3, O 12 'CH3COOH' acetic acid C 2, H 4, O 2 '(NH4)3PO4' ammonium phosphate N 3, H 12, P 1, O 4 'K4[Fe(CN)6]' potassium ferrocyanide K 4, Fe 1, C 6, N 6 'O2' oxygen gas O 2 'Fe' a single element Fe 1

docs.title: See how a formula was read
docs.text:
parse_formula returns the atom counts chemhelper will use. It is the quickest way to check that a formula means what you intended.

>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('Al2(SO4)3'))
{'Al': 2, 'S': 3, 'O': 12}
>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('CH3COOH'))
{'C': 2, 'H': 4, 'O': 2}
>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('K4[Fe(CN)6]'))
{'K': 4, 'Fe': 1, 'C': 6, 'N': 6}

docs.title: Capitalization matters
docs.text:
Co is cobalt. CO is carbon monoxide. The parser cannot guess which you meant, so type symbols exactly as they appear on the periodic table.

>>> compounds.mass('Co')
58.93
>>> compounds.mass('CO')
28.01

docs.title: What is not supported
docs.text: You might write Problem Write this instead 'CuSO4·5H2O' or 'CuSO4.5H2O' The hydrate dot is not understood. 'CuSO4(H2O)5' '2H2O' Leading coefficients are not understood. Use 'H2O' and multiply the result by 2. 'SO4 2-' or 'Na+' Charges are not understood. Leave the charge off: 'SO4', 'Na'. An electron's mass is negligible here. 'h2o' or 'NACL' Symbols must be capitalized correctly. 'H2O', 'NaCl' 'H₂O' Unicode subscripts are not understood. 'H2O' 'Pu' Elements past uranium are not included. Not available yet; see the roadmap. Isotopes such as deuterium No isotope data. See adding your own element.

docs.title: Error messages
docs.text:
A formula the parser cannot read raises ValueError with a message that says what is wrong.

An unknown or mis-capitalized element:

>>> compounds.mass('Xy2')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unknown element 'Xy' in formula 'Xy2'
>>> compounds.mass('NACL')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unknown element 'A' in formula 'NACL'

Reading the second error

In 'NACL' the parser reads N (nitrogen), then A, which is not an element. All-caps formulas usually fail on the first letter that is not itself a one-letter element.

Unbalanced parentheses:

>>> compounds.mass('Ca(OH2')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unbalanced parentheses in formula 'Ca(OH2'

A character that does not belong in a formula:

>>> compounds.mass('h2o')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unexpected character 'h' in formula 'h2o'
>>> compounds.mass('CuSO4.5H2O')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unexpected character '.' in formula 'CuSO4.5H2O'

An empty string:

>>> compounds.mass('')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Empty formula ''

docs.title: A caution about look-alike formulas
docs.text:
The parser checks that every symbol is a real element. It does not check that the compound exists. A typo that happens to spell real elements is accepted:

>>> compounds.mass('HO2')
33.01

When an answer looks wrong, run parse_formula on your string first.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Version Python 3.10 or newer pandas 1.3 or newer (installed automatically)

chemhelper is pure Python and runs anywhere pandas does: Windows, macOS and Linux.

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install chemhelper

To upgrade an existing installation:

pip install --upgrade chemhelper

Version 1.0 is new

If pip gives you version 0.4, the 1.0 release has not reached PyPI yet. Install it from GitHub as shown below.

docs.title: Install from GitHub
docs.text:
This installs the latest code on the master branch:

pip install git+https://github.com/drosenman/chemhelper.git

docs.title: Install in a notebook
docs.text:
In Jupyter or Google Colab, run this in a cell:

%pip install chemhelper

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
>>> import chemhelper
>>> chemhelper.__version__
'1.0.0'
>>> from chemhelper import compounds
>>> compounds.mass('H2O')
18.02

If you see a version number and a molar mass for water, you're ready for the Quickstart.

docs.title: Import the modules
docs.text:
chemhelper has four modules. Import the ones you need:

from chemhelper import elements, compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

Importing the package also loads all four, so this works too:

import chemhelper

chemhelper.compounds.mass('H2O')
Module What it does Guide elements Periodic table data elements compounds Molar mass and composition compounds conversions Grams, moles and molarity conversions ideal_gas PV = nRT ideal_gas

docs.title: Install for development
docs.text:
To change chemhelper itself, clone the repository and install it in editable mode with the test and documentation tools:

git clone https://github.com/drosenman/chemhelper.git
cd chemhelper
pip install -e ".[test,docs]"

See Contributing for the rest of the workflow.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This page takes about five minutes and touches every module. Each example can be pasted into a Python prompt or a notebook cell.

>>> from chemhelper import elements, compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

docs.title: 1. Look up an element
docs.text:
Every element from hydrogen to uranium is available by its symbol.

>>> print(elements.Fe)
Element: Iron, Fe
Atomic Number: 26
Mass: 55.85
>>> elements.Fe.mass
55.85
>>> elements.elements['Na'].name
'Sodium'

More in the elements guide.

docs.title: 2. Find a molar mass
docs.text:
Write the formula as a string, the way it appears in a textbook.

>>> compounds.mass('H2O')
18.02
>>> compounds.mass('C6H12O6')
180.16
>>> compounds.mass('Al2(SO4)3')
342.17

docs.title: 3. Show the work
docs.text:
Add _steps to the function name to print the worked solution.

>>> compounds.mass_steps('Al2(SO4)3')
Al2(SO4)3
Al: 2 x 26.98 = 53.96
S: 3 x 32.07 = 96.21
O: 12 x 16.0 = 192.0

Mass Al2(SO4)3 = 53.96 + 96.21 + 192.0 = 342.17

Every solver in chemhelper has a _steps twin. See Answers and worked solutions.

docs.title: 4. Percent composition
docs.text:
>>> compounds.percent_composition('C6H12O6')
C          39.999
H           6.714
O          53.287
Total:    100.000
Name: C6H12O6, dtype: float64

The result is a pandas Series, so you can pull out one element:

>>> float(compounds.percent_composition('C6H12O6')['C'])
39.999

docs.title: 5. Convert grams and moles
docs.text:
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(90.1, 'H2O')
5.0
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(0.25, 'NaCl')
14.61
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(90.1, 'H2O')
90.1g H2O x 1 mole H2O/18.02g H2O = 5.0 moles H2O

docs.title: 6. Work with solutions
docs.text:
What is the molarity when 10 g of NaOH is dissolved to make 0.25 L of solution?

>>> conversions.molarity(0.25, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
1.0
>>> conversions.molarity_steps(0.25, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
10g NaOH x 1 mole NaOH/40.0g NaOH = 0.25 moles NaOH
0.25 moles/0.25 L = 1 M

How many grams of NaCl are in 2 L of a 0.5 M solution?

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.5, 2, 'NaCl')
58.44

docs.title: 7. Solve the ideal gas law
docs.text:
Name the variable you want and give the other three.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', V=5, n=4, T=300)
19.7
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('P', V=5, n=4, T=300)
PV = nRT
P = nRT/V
P = 4 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 300 K / 5 L = 19.7 atm

Inputs can use other units, and a mass can stand in for moles:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', substance='CO2', m=44.01, P=740, Punits='torr', T=25, Tunits='C')
25.14

docs.title: Answers and worked solutions
docs.text:
chemhelper is built around one idea: every solver comes as a pair.

  • The plain function returns the answer, so you can store it or use it in another calculation.
  • The function with _steps added to its name prints the worked solution and returns nothing.

Both take exactly the same arguments.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(36.04, 'H2O')
2.0

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(36.04, 'H2O')
36.04g H2O x 1 mole H2O/18.02g H2O = 2.0 moles H2O

docs.title: All the pairs
docs.text: Returns the answer Prints the solution What it solves compounds.mass compounds.mass_steps Molar mass compounds.composition compounds.composition_steps Grams of each element per mole compounds.percent_composition compounds.percent_composition_steps Percent by mass of each element conversions.grams_to_moles conversions.grams_to_moles_steps Grams → moles conversions.moles_to_grams conversions.moles_to_grams_steps Moles → grams conversions.molarity conversions.molarity_steps Molarity of a solution conversions.molarity_to_moles conversions.molarity_to_moles_steps Moles of solute in a solution conversions.molarity_to_grams conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps Grams of solute in a solution ideal_gas.ideal_gas ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps PV = nRT for any variable

docs.title: Solutions build on each other
docs.text:
A _steps function shows every calculation the answer depends on. Asking for the grams of solute in a solution prints the moles first, then the molar mass, then the final conversion:

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps(0.5, 2, 'NaCl')
0.5 moles/L x 2 L = 1 moles
NaCl
Na: 22.99
Cl: 35.45

Mass NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44
1 moles x 58.44 grams/mole = 58.44 grams

Percent composition prints the molar mass, then the mass each element contributes, then each percentage:

>>> compounds.percent_composition_steps('H2O')
H2O
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
O: 16.0

Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02

H          2.016
O         16.000
Total:    18.020
Name: H2O, dtype: float64
H: 100 x 2.016g H/18.02g H2O = 11.19%
O: 100 x 16.0g O/18.02g H2O = 88.81%

docs.title: _steps functions return nothing
docs.text:
They print. If you assign the result, you get None:

>>> result = compounds.mass_steps('H2O')
H2O
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
O: 16.0

Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02
>>> print(result)
None

To keep the number, call the plain function:

>>> result = compounds.mass('H2O')
>>> result
18.02

docs.title: Capture a solution as text
docs.text:
To put a worked solution in a file, a web page or a message, capture what the function prints with the standard library:

>>> import contextlib, io
>>> buffer = io.StringIO()
>>> with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buffer):
...     conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(36.04, 'H2O')
>>> solution = buffer.getvalue()
>>> solution
'36.04g H2O x 1 mole H2O/18.02g H2O = 2.0 moles H2O\n'

The Cookbook wraps this in a reusable helper.

docs.title: A good way to use the pair
docs.text:
1. Ask the student for their answer.
  2. Call the plain function to check it.
  3. If it is wrong, call the _steps twin and compare line by line to find the first step where their work differs.

The tutoring session tutorial walks through this.

docs.title: Units and rounding
docs.text:
chemhelper works with plain numbers. It does not attach units to them, so you need to know which units each function expects and which it returns.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

docs.title: What goes in and what comes out
docs.text: Quantity Unit Used by Mass grams (g) conversions, ideal_gas (m) Amount moles (mol) conversions, ideal_gas (n) Molar mass grams per mole (g/mol) compounds, elements Volume of solution liters (L) conversions Concentration moles per liter (M) conversions Gas volume liters by default; milliliters with Vunits='mL' ideal_gas Pressure atmospheres by default; Punits may be 'torr', 'mmHg' or 'kPa' ideal_gas Temperature kelvin by default; Celsius with Tunits='C' ideal_gas

docs.title: Volumes in conversions are always liters
docs.text:
The molarity functions have no unit option. Convert milliliters yourself by dividing by 1000:

>>> conversions.molarity(250 / 1000, moles=0.05)
0.2

docs.title: Unit options in ideal_gas describe your inputs
docs.text:
Punits, Vunits and Tunits tell ideal_gas what units the values you give are in. The answer always comes back in the base unit:

You solve for The result is in 'P' atm 'V' L 'n' mol 'T' K 
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=760, Punits='torr', V=500, Vunits='mL', T=25, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
0.0204

To get an answer in another unit, convert it afterwards:

>>> p_atm = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', n=2, V=10, T=300)
>>> p_atm
4.93
>>> round(p_atm * 760, 1)
3746.8
>>> t_kelvin = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', P=1, V=12, n=0.5)
>>> round(t_kelvin - 273.15, 2)
19.18

docs.title: Conversion factors used
docs.text: Conversion Factor torr or mmHg → atm divide by 760 kPa → atm divide by 101.325 mL → L divide by 1000 °C → K add 273.15

docs.title: The gas constant
docs.text:
ideal_gas uses R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), the three-significant-figure value printed in most general chemistry textbooks. It is available as a constant:

>>> ideal_gas.R
0.0821

Because R has three significant figures, ideal gas answers are reliable to about three significant figures, however many decimals you ask for.

docs.title: Rounding
docs.text:
Results are rounded so they look like textbook answers. Each function rounds only its final result.

Function Result is rounded to compounds.mass 2 decimals compounds.composition 4 decimals per element; 2 for the total compounds.percent_composition 3 decimals conversions.grams_to_moles 2 decimals conversions.moles_to_grams 2 decimals conversions.molarity not rounded conversions.molarity_to_moles not rounded conversions.molarity_to_grams 2 decimals ideal_gas.ideal_gas decimals argument, 2 by default

docs.title: Numbers in printed solutions
docs.text: _steps functions show intermediate quantities to four significant figures (six in ideal_gas_steps), so small amounts such as 0.00375 mol stay visible. Masses in grams and molar masses are shown to two decimals.

docs.title: Molar masses are rounded before they are used in conversions
docs.text: The conversions functions and the mass option of ideal_gas use the two-decimal molar mass from compounds.mass, the same number a student would read off their own calculation.

docs.title: Very small amounts
docs.text:
Two decimals is not enough for very small quantities. Five milligrams of water is a real amount, but it rounds to zero moles:

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(0.005, 'H2O')
0.0

When you need more precision, divide by the molar mass yourself:

>>> round(0.005 / compounds.mass('H2O'), 6)
0.000277

docs.title: Choosing decimals for gas problems
docs.text:
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1)
22.43
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1, decimals=4)
22.4256
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1, decimals=0)
22.0

docs.title: Significant figures
docs.text: chemhelper does not track significant figures. It rounds to a fixed number of decimals. Apply your course's significant-figure rules to the final answer yourself. This is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Floating-point tails
docs.text:
The functions that do not round can return values such as 0.30000000000000004. That is ordinary floating-point arithmetic, not a chemistry error. Round the result when you display it:

>>> conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.1, 3)
0.30000000000000004
>>> round(conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.1, 3), 4)
0.3

docs.title: compounds
docs.text:
The compounds module answers three questions about a chemical formula:

  1. What is its molar mass?
  2. How much of that mass does each element contribute?
  3. What percent of the mass is each element?
>>> from chemhelper import compounds

Every function takes a formula string. See Writing formulas for what is accepted.

Function Returns Twin that prints the solution parse_formula atom counts none mass molar mass mass_steps composition grams of each element per mole composition_steps percent_composition percent by mass of each element percent_composition_steps

docs.title: parse_formula
docs.text:
compounds.parse_formula(chemical)

Counts the atoms of each element in a formula. The other functions in this module all start by calling it.

Arguments

Name Type Description chemical str A chemical formula, such as 'Ca(OH)2'

Returns

An OrderedDict mapping each element symbol to its number of atoms, in the order the elements first appear in the formula.

Raises

ValueError for an unknown element, unbalanced parentheses, an unexpected character, or an empty formula. The message names the problem.

Examples

>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('H2O'))
{'H': 2, 'O': 1}
>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('Ca(OH)2'))
{'Ca': 1, 'O': 2, 'H': 2}
>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('Al2(SO4)3'))
{'Al': 2, 'S': 3, 'O': 12}

An element that appears more than once is counted together:

>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('CH3COOH'))
{'C': 2, 'H': 4, 'O': 2}
>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('NH4NO3'))
{'N': 2, 'H': 4, 'O': 3}

Nested groups multiply through:

>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('K4[Fe(CN)6]'))
{'K': 4, 'Fe': 1, 'C': 6, 'N': 6}

Count the total number of atoms in a formula unit:

>>> sum(compounds.parse_formula('C6H12O6').values())
24

Get the mole ratio of two elements:

>>> counts = compounds.parse_formula('Al2(SO4)3')
>>> counts['O'] / counts['Al']
6.0

docs.title: mass
docs.text:
compounds.mass(chemical)

The molar mass of a compound: the mass in grams of one mole of it.

Arguments

Name Type Description chemical str A chemical formula

Returns

A float: the molar mass in g/mol, rounded to 2 decimals.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

For each element, multiply its atomic mass by its number of atoms, then add the results:

\[ M = \sum_i n_i \, m_i \]

where \(n_i\) is the number of atoms of element \(i\) and \(m_i\) is its atomic mass. For water: \(2 \times 1.008 + 16.00 = 18.016\), which rounds to 18.02 g/mol.

Examples

>>> compounds.mass('H2O')
18.02
>>> compounds.mass('NaCl')
58.44
>>> compounds.mass('C6H12O6')
180.16
>>> compounds.mass('Ca(OH)2')
74.1
>>> compounds.mass('Al2(SO4)3')
342.17

A single element works too. For a diatomic gas, write the molecule:

>>> compounds.mass('O')
16.0
>>> compounds.mass('O2')
32.0

Molar masses of several compounds at once:

>>> {formula: compounds.mass(formula) for formula in ['HCl', 'H2SO4', 'HNO3']}
{'HCl': 36.46, 'H2SO4': 98.09, 'HNO3': 63.02}

docs.title: mass_steps
docs.text:
compounds.mass_steps(chemical)

Prints the molar mass calculation one element at a time, then the sum.

Arguments

The same as mass.

Prints

  1. The formula.
  2. One line per element. If there is more than one atom, the line shows the count times the atomic mass.
  3. The contributions added together, with the molar mass rounded to 2 decimals.

Examples

>>> compounds.mass_steps('H2O')
H2O
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
O: 16.0

Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02

>>> compounds.mass_steps('C6H12O6')
C6H12O6
C: 6 x 12.01 = 72.06
H: 12 x 1.008 = 12.096
O: 6 x 16.0 = 96.0

Mass C6H12O6 = 72.06 + 12.096 + 96.0 = 180.16

With parentheses, each line shows the total count of that element in the whole formula. Calcium hydroxide has two oxygens and two hydrogens:

>>> compounds.mass_steps('Ca(OH)2')
Ca(OH)2
Ca: 40.08
O: 2 x 16.0 = 32.0
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016

Mass Ca(OH)2 = 40.08 + 32.0 + 2.016 = 74.1

docs.title: composition
docs.text:
compounds.composition(chemical)

The mass each element contributes to one mole of the compound.

Arguments

Name Type Description chemical str A chemical formula

Returns

A pandas Series named after the formula. There is one entry per element, giving the grams of that element in one mole of the compound, followed by a 'Total:' entry with the molar mass.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

Examples

>>> compounds.composition('H2O')
H          2.016
O         16.000
Total:    18.020
Name: H2O, dtype: float64
>>> compounds.composition('C6H12O6')
C          72.060
H          12.096
O          96.000
Total:    180.160
Name: C6H12O6, dtype: float64

Pick out one element, or the total:

>>> comp = compounds.composition('C6H12O6')
>>> float(comp['C'])
72.06
>>> float(comp['Total:'])
180.16

Drop the total to keep only the elements:

>>> comp.drop('Total:')
C    72.060
H    12.096
O    96.000
Name: C6H12O6, dtype: float64

Repeated elements are combined into one entry:

>>> compounds.composition('CH3COOH')
C         24.020
H          4.032
O         32.000
Total:    60.050
Name: CH3COOH, dtype: float64

Why float(...)?

Values taken from a pandas Series are NumPy numbers. They calculate like ordinary numbers; wrapping one in float() only changes how it prints.

docs.title: composition_steps
docs.text:
compounds.composition_steps(chemical)

Prints the molar mass calculation from mass_steps, then the composition table.

Example

>>> compounds.composition_steps('H2O')
H2O
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
O: 16.0

Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02

H          2.016
O         16.000
Total:    18.020
Name: H2O, dtype: float64

docs.title: percent_composition
docs.text:
compounds.percent_composition(chemical)

The percent by mass of each element in the compound.

Arguments

Name Type Description chemical str A chemical formula

Returns

A pandas Series named after the formula. There is one entry per element, giving its percent of the compound's mass rounded to 3 decimals, followed by a 'Total:' entry that is always 100.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

\[ \%\,\text{element} = \frac{\text{mass of the element in one mole}}{\text{molar mass of the compound}} \times 100 \]

For hydrogen in water: \(2.016 / 18.016 \times 100 = 11.19\%\).

Examples

>>> compounds.percent_composition('H2O')
H          11.19
O          88.81
Total:    100.00
Name: H2O, dtype: float64
>>> compounds.percent_composition('C6H12O6')
C          39.999
H           6.714
O          53.287
Total:    100.000
Name: C6H12O6, dtype: float64
>>> compounds.percent_composition('Al2(SO4)3')
Al         15.770
S          28.118
O          56.112
Total:    100.000
Name: Al2(SO4)3, dtype: float64

The percent of one element:

>>> float(compounds.percent_composition('NaCl')['Na'])
39.339

Which element makes up most of the mass?

>>> compounds.percent_composition('Fe2O3').drop('Total:').idxmax()
'Fe'

Compare nitrogen content in three fertilizers:

>>> for formula in ['NH3', 'NH4NO3', '(NH4)2SO4']:
...     print(formula, float(compounds.percent_composition(formula)['N']))
NH3 82.247
NH4NO3 35.002
(NH4)2SO4 21.203

Percentages may not add to exactly 100

Each percentage is rounded separately, so the element entries can sum to 99.999 or 100.001. The 'Total:' entry is set to 100.

docs.title: percent_composition_steps
docs.text:
compounds.percent_composition_steps(chemical)

Prints the complete solution: the molar mass calculation, the mass each element contributes, and then each percentage.

Example

>>> compounds.percent_composition_steps('H2O')
H2O
H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
O: 16.0

Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02

H          2.016
O         16.000
Total:    18.020
Name: H2O, dtype: float64
H: 100 x 2.016g H/18.02g H2O = 11.19%
O: 100 x 16.0g O/18.02g H2O = 88.81%

>>> compounds.percent_composition_steps('CaCO3')
CaCO3
Ca: 40.08
C: 12.01
O: 3 x 16.0 = 48.0

Mass CaCO3 = 40.08 + 12.01 + 48.0 = 100.09

Ca         40.08
C          12.01
O          48.00
Total:    100.09
Name: CaCO3, dtype: float64
Ca: 100 x 40.08g Ca/100.09g CaCO3 = 40.04%
C: 100 x 12.01g C/100.09g CaCO3 = 12.00%
O: 100 x 48.0g O/100.09g CaCO3 = 47.96%

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Wrong capitalization. 'CO' is carbon monoxide and 'Co' is cobalt. 'co' is an error.

Forgetting the subscript on diatomic elements. Oxygen gas is 'O2', not 'O'. The same goes for H₂, N₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂.

Writing a hydrate with a dot. Use parentheses: 'CuSO4(H2O)5'.

>>> compounds.mass('CuSO4(H2O)5')
249.7

Expecting _steps to return the number. _steps functions print and return None. Call the plain function to get a value.

See Writing formulas for the full list of what the parser accepts and the error messages it gives.

docs.title: conversions
docs.text:
The conversions module moves between the three quantities at the center of stoichiometry: grams, moles and molarity.

>>> from chemhelper import conversions

flowchart LR
    G["grams of substance"]
    N["moles of substance"]
    M["molarity of solution"]
    G -- "grams_to_moles" --> N
    N -- "moles_to_grams" --> G
    N -- "molarity" --> M
    M -- "molarity_to_moles" --> N
    G -- "molarity (with mass)" --> M
    M -- "molarity_to_grams" --> G
Function Converts Twin that prints the solution grams_to_moles grams → moles grams_to_moles_steps moles_to_grams moles → grams moles_to_grams_steps molarity moles (or grams) and volume → molarity molarity_steps molarity_to_moles molarity and volume → moles molarity_to_moles_steps molarity_to_grams molarity and volume → grams molarity_to_grams_steps

Units on this page

Mass is in grams, amount in moles, volume in liters and concentration in moles per liter (M). To use milliliters, divide by 1000 first. See Units and rounding.

docs.title: grams_to_moles
docs.text:
conversions.grams_to_moles(mass, chemical)

Converts a mass of a substance to moles.

Arguments

Name Type Description mass number Mass of the sample in grams chemical str Chemical formula of the substance

Returns

A float: the number of moles, rounded to 2 decimals.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

\[ n = \frac{m}{M} \]

where \(m\) is the mass in grams and \(M\) is the molar mass from compounds.mass.

Examples

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(36.04, 'H2O')
2.0
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(100, 'NaCl')
1.71
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(45.0, 'C6H12O6')
0.25

Small samples round to zero

The result has two decimals, so anything under 0.005 mol becomes 0.0. For small samples divide by the molar mass yourself:

>>> from chemhelper import compounds
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(0.05, 'C6H12O6')
0.0
>>> round(0.05 / compounds.mass('C6H12O6'), 6)
0.000278

docs.title: grams_to_moles_steps
docs.text:
conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(mass, chemical)

Prints the conversion as a single dimensional-analysis line: the mass, times one mole over the molar mass.

Arguments

The same as grams_to_moles.

Examples

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(36.04, 'H2O')
36.04g H2O x 1 mole H2O/18.02g H2O = 2.0 moles H2O
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(100, 'NaCl')
100g NaCl x 1 mole NaCl/58.44g NaCl = 1.71 moles NaCl

docs.title: moles_to_grams
docs.text:
conversions.moles_to_grams(moles, chemical)

Converts moles of a substance to grams.

Arguments

Name Type Description moles number Amount of substance in moles chemical str Chemical formula of the substance

Returns

A float: the mass in grams, rounded to 2 decimals.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

\[ m = n \times M \]

Examples

>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(2, 'H2O')
36.04
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(0.25, 'NaCl')
14.61
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(1.5, 'CO2')
66.02

docs.title: moles_to_grams_steps
docs.text:
conversions.moles_to_grams_steps(moles, chemical)

Prints the molar mass calculation, then the moles times the molar mass.

Arguments

The same as moles_to_grams.

Example

>>> conversions.moles_to_grams_steps(0.25, 'NaCl')
NaCl
Na: 22.99
Cl: 35.45

Mass NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44
0.25 moles x 58.44 grams/mole = 14.61 grams

docs.title: molarity
docs.text:
conversions.molarity(volume, mass=None, chemical=None, moles=None)

The molarity of a solution: moles of solute per liter of solution.

There are two ways to call it:

  • give the moles of solute, or
  • give the mass of solute together with its formula.

Arguments

Name Type Description volume number Volume of the solution in liters mass number, optional Mass of solute in grams chemical str, optional Formula of the solute. Required with mass. moles number, optional Moles of solute

If you give moles, then mass and chemical are ignored.

Returns

A float: the molarity in mol/L. It is not rounded.

Raises

ValueError if you give neither moles nor both mass and chemical, or if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

\[ M = \frac{n}{V} \]

With a mass, the moles are found first as \(n = m / M_\text{molar}\).

Examples

From moles:

>>> conversions.molarity(0.5, moles=1)
2.0
>>> conversions.molarity(2, moles=0.5)
0.25

From a mass of solute:

>>> conversions.molarity(2, mass=58.44, chemical='NaCl')
0.5
>>> conversions.molarity(0.25, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
1.0

volume is the first argument, so name the others:

>>> round(conversions.molarity(volume=0.1, mass=4.9, chemical='H2SO4'), 3)
0.5

Volumes in milliliters need converting:

>>> conversions.molarity(250 / 1000, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
1.0

Leaving out the formula is an error:

>>> conversions.molarity(1, mass=10)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Give either moles, or both mass and chemical.

docs.title: molarity_steps
docs.text:
conversions.molarity_steps(volume, mass=None, chemical=None, moles=None)

Prints the molarity calculation. If you give a mass, the grams-to-moles conversion is printed first.

Arguments

The same as molarity.

Examples

>>> conversions.molarity_steps(0.25, mass=10, chemical='NaOH')
10g NaOH x 1 mole NaOH/40.0g NaOH = 0.25 moles NaOH
0.25 moles/0.25 L = 1 M

>>> conversions.molarity_steps(0.5, moles=1)
1 moles/0.5 L = 2 M

docs.title: molarity_to_moles
docs.text:
conversions.molarity_to_moles(M, volume)

The moles of solute in a given volume of solution.

Arguments

Name Type Description M number Concentration in mol/L volume number Volume of solution in liters

Returns

A float: moles of solute. It is not rounded.

How it is calculated

\[ n = M \times V \]

Examples

>>> conversions.molarity_to_moles(2, 0.5)
1.0
>>> conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.25, 0.1)
0.025

This function does not need to know what the solute is, so it takes no formula.

docs.title: molarity_to_moles_steps
docs.text:
conversions.molarity_to_moles_steps(M, volume)

Prints the molarity times the volume.

Example

>>> conversions.molarity_to_moles_steps(2, 0.5)
2 moles/L x 0.5 L = 1 moles

docs.title: molarity_to_grams
docs.text:
conversions.molarity_to_grams(molarity, volume, chemical)

The grams of solute in a given volume of solution. Use it to answer "how much do I weigh out to make this solution?"

Arguments

Name Type Description molarity number Concentration in mol/L volume number Volume of solution in liters chemical str Formula of the solute

Returns

A float: the mass of solute in grams, rounded to 2 decimals.

Raises

ValueError if the formula cannot be read.

How it is calculated

\[ m = M \times V \times M_\text{molar} \]

Examples

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.5, 2, 'NaCl')
58.44
>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.1, 0.25, 'NaOH')
1.0
>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(1.0, 0.5, 'C6H12O6')
90.08

docs.title: molarity_to_grams_steps
docs.text:
conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps(molarity, volume, chemical)

Prints the whole chain: molarity to moles, the molar mass, then moles to grams.

Arguments

The same as molarity_to_grams.

Example

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps(0.5, 2, 'NaCl')
0.5 moles/L x 2 L = 1 moles
NaCl
Na: 22.99
Cl: 35.45

Mass NaCl = 22.99 + 35.45 = 58.44
1 moles x 58.44 grams/mole = 58.44 grams

docs.title: Combining conversions
docs.text:
The functions are designed to chain. Each returns a number the next one accepts.

Dilution. 50 mL of 2.0 M HCl is diluted to 400 mL. What is the new concentration? The moles of solute do not change, so find them, then divide by the new volume:

>>> moles = conversions.molarity_to_moles(2.0, 0.050)
>>> conversions.molarity(0.400, moles=moles)
0.25

Grams of one substance to grams of another. For 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O, how many grams of water form from 8.0 g of H₂? Convert to moles, apply the mole ratio from the balanced equation, and convert back:

>>> moles_h2 = conversions.grams_to_moles(8.0, 'H2')
>>> moles_h2o = moles_h2 * 2 / 2
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(moles_h2o, 'H2O')
71.36

chemhelper does not balance equations or read mole ratios for you. You supply the ratio.

More worked problems are in the solutions tutorial and the Cookbook.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Using milliliters. Every volume here is in liters. 250 mL is 0.25.

Using the volume of solvent. Molarity is defined per liter of solution, the final volume after the solute has dissolved.

Passing mass without chemical. molarity needs the formula to turn grams into moles.

Positional arguments in molarity. The order is volume, mass, chemical, moles. Naming the arguments, as in molarity(0.5, moles=1), avoids mixing them up.

docs.title: elements
docs.text:
The elements module holds the periodic table data that the rest of chemhelper is built on: the symbol, name, atomic number and atomic mass of every element from hydrogen (1) to uranium (92).

>>> from chemhelper import elements

Two things are called elements

elements is the module. Inside it is a pandas Series that is also called elements. So elements.Fe is an attribute of the module, and elements.elements['Fe'] is a lookup in the Series. Both give you the same object.

docs.title: The Element class
docs.text:
class Element(symbol, name, atomic_number, mass)

An Element is a small record describing one element.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Attribute Type Description Example for iron symbol str Chemical symbol 'Fe' name str Element name 'Iron' atomic_number int Number of protons 26 mass float Atomic mass in g/mol 55.85 
>>> iron = elements.Fe
>>> iron.symbol
'Fe'
>>> iron.name
'Iron'
>>> iron.atomic_number
26
>>> iron.mass
55.85

What mass means

mass is the molar mass of the element in grams per mole. The same number is the average mass of one atom in atomic mass units (amu).

docs.title: Printing an element
docs.text:
print gives a readable summary. Typing the name alone at a prompt gives a compact form that shows how the object was built.

>>> print(elements.Ca)
Element: Calcium, Ca
Atomic Number: 20
Mass: 40.08
>>> elements.Ca
Element('Ca', 'Calcium', 20, 40.08)

More examples:

>>> print(elements.H)
Element: Hydrogen, H
Atomic Number: 1
Mass: 1.008
>>> elements.Ti.name
'Titanium'
>>> elements.Ag.mass
107.87
>>> elements.K.atomic_number
19

docs.title: Four ways to get an element
By symbol, as a module attribute
docs.text:
Every element is a variable in the module, named by its symbol. This is the shortest form when you know the element as you write the code.

>>> elements.Na
Element('Na', 'Sodium', 11, 22.99)
>>> elements.Na.mass
22.99

docs.title: By symbol, from the elements Series
docs.text:
Use this when the symbol is in a variable.

>>> symbol = 'Cl'
>>> elements.elements[symbol]
Element('Cl', 'Chlorine', 17, 35.45)
>>> elements.elements[symbol].mass
35.45

docs.title: By atomic number
docs.text:
element_objects is a list in order of atomic number. Lists count from zero, so the element with atomic number Z is at position Z − 1.

>>> elements.element_objects[0]
Element('H', 'Hydrogen', 1, 1.008)
>>> elements.element_objects[26 - 1]
Element('Fe', 'Iron', 26, 55.85)

element_table is indexed by atomic number directly:

>>> elements.element_table.loc[26]
Atomic Number
Symbol       Fe
Name       Iron
Mass      55.85
Name: 26, dtype: object

docs.title: By name
docs.text:
Search the Name column of element_table:

>>> table = elements.element_table
>>> table[table['Name'] == 'Gold']
Atomic Number Symbol  Name    Mass
79                Au  Gold  196.97

docs.title: The elements Series
docs.text:
elements.elements is a pandas Series of all 92 Element objects, indexed by symbol.

>>> len(elements.elements)
92
>>> elements.elements['O']
Element('O', 'Oxygen', 8, 16.0)
>>> 'Fe' in elements.elements.index
True
>>> 'Xx' in elements.elements.index
False

Look up several elements at once:

>>> [e.name for e in elements.elements[['H', 'C', 'N', 'O']]]
['Hydrogen', 'Carbon', 'Nitrogen', 'Oxygen']

Loop over all of them:

>>> [e.symbol for e in elements.elements if e.mass > 220]
['Rn', 'Fr', 'Ra', 'Ac', 'Th', 'Pa', 'U']

docs.title: element_index
docs.text:
A list of the 92 symbols in order of atomic number.

>>> elements.element_index[:10]
['H', 'He', 'Li', 'Be', 'B', 'C', 'N', 'O', 'F', 'Ne']
>>> len(elements.element_index)
92
>>> elements.element_index.index('Fe') + 1
26

The last line finds an atomic number from a symbol: the position in the list, plus one.

docs.title: element_objects
docs.text:
A list of the 92 Element objects in order of atomic number.

>>> elements.element_objects[:3]
[Element('H', 'Hydrogen', 1, 1.008), Element('He', 'Helium', 2, 4.0026), Element('Li', 'Lithium', 3, 6.94)]
>>> elements.element_objects[-1]
Element('U', 'Uranium', 92, 238.03)

docs.title: element_table
docs.text:
A pandas DataFrame with one row per element. The index is the atomic number and the columns are Symbol, Name and Mass.

>>> elements.element_table.head()
Atomic Number Symbol       Name   Mass
1                  H   Hydrogen   1.01
2                 He     Helium   4.00
3                 Li    Lithium   6.94
4                 Be  Beryllium   9.01
5                  B      Boron  10.81
>>> elements.element_table.shape
(92, 3)

Masses in the table are rounded to two decimals

element_table is meant for display, so its Mass column is rounded to two decimals. The Element objects keep the stored value, and that is what calculations use.

>>> elements.H.mass
1.008
>>> float(elements.element_table.loc[1, 'Mass'])
1.01

Because it is a DataFrame, all of pandas is available.

The five heaviest elements:

>>> elements.element_table.sort_values('Mass', ascending=False).head()
Atomic Number Symbol          Name    Mass
92                 U       Uranium  238.03
90                Th       Thorium  232.04
91                Pa  Protactinium  231.04
89                Ac      Actinium  227.00
88                Ra        Radium  226.00

The noble gases:

>>> table = elements.element_table
>>> table[table['Symbol'].isin(['He', 'Ne', 'Ar', 'Kr', 'Xe', 'Rn'])]
Atomic Number Symbol     Name    Mass
2                 He   Helium    4.00
10                Ne     Neon   20.18
18                Ar    Argon   39.95
36                Kr  Krypton   83.80
54                Xe    Xenon  131.29
86                Rn    Radon  222.00

Elements whose names start with "C":

>>> table[table['Name'].str.startswith('C')]['Name'].tolist()
['Carbon', 'Chlorine', 'Calcium', 'Chromium', 'Cobalt', 'Copper', 'Cadmium', 'Cesium', 'Cerium']

The period 2 elements, by atomic number:

>>> table.loc[3:10]
Atomic Number Symbol       Name   Mass
3                 Li    Lithium   6.94
4                 Be  Beryllium   9.01
5                  B      Boron  10.81
6                  C     Carbon  12.01
7                  N   Nitrogen  14.01
8                  O     Oxygen  16.00
9                  F   Fluorine  19.00
10                Ne       Neon  20.18

Save the whole table to a spreadsheet-friendly file:

elements.element_table.to_csv('elements.csv')

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
• Coverage. Elements 1 to 92. Elements past uranium are not included yet.
  • Masses. The rounded values printed on most classroom periodic tables, usually two decimal places. Hydrogen (1.008) and helium (4.0026) carry more.
  • Radioactive elements. Elements with no stable isotope (Tc, Pm, and Po through Ac) use the mass number of a long-lived isotope, as periodic tables do.
  • Your textbook may differ slightly. Standard atomic masses are revised from time to time, so a recent table can differ from these values in the last digit. The periodic table page lists every value chemhelper uses.

docs.title: Add your own element
docs.text:
The Element class is public, so you can create elements that are not in the table. A common reason is an isotope, such as deuterium.

>>> D = elements.Element('D', 'Deuterium', 1, 2.014)
>>> print(D)
Element: Deuterium, D
Atomic Number: 1
Mass: 2.014

To use a new element inside formulas, add it to the elements Series. The formula parser looks symbols up there.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds
>>> elements.elements['D'] = D
>>> compounds.mass('D2O')
20.03
>>> compounds.mass('H2O')
18.02

This lasts until Python restarts

The addition lives in memory only, and it does not update element_index, element_objects or element_table. A symbol must be one capital letter optionally followed by one lowercase letter, or the parser will not recognize it.

docs.title: ideal_gas
docs.text:
The ideal_gas module solves the ideal gas law for any one of its four variables.

\[ PV = nRT \] 
>>> from chemhelper import ideal_gas
Symbol Quantity Argument Default unit \(P\) pressure P atm \(V\) volume V L \(n\) amount of gas n mol \(T\) absolute temperature T K \(R\) gas constant fixed 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K)

The module has two functions, which take the same arguments:

Function What it does ideal_gas Returns the answer ideal_gas_steps Prints the worked solution

docs.title: ideal_gas
docs.text:
ideal_gas.ideal_gas(solve_for, substance=None, P=None, V=None, n=None, T=None,
                    m=None, decimals=2, Tunits='K', Vunits='L', Punits='atm')

Name the variable you want with solve_for, and give the other three.

Arguments

Name Type Default Description solve_for 'P', 'V', 'n' or 'T' required The variable to solve for substance str None Formula of the gas. Needed only when you give m. P number None Pressure, in Punits V number None Volume, in Vunits n number None Amount of gas in moles T number None Temperature, in Tunits m number None Mass of gas in grams. Used to find n. decimals int 2 Decimal places in the result Tunits 'K' or 'C' 'K' Units of the T you give Vunits 'L' or 'mL' 'L' Units of the V you give Punits 'atm', 'torr', 'mmHg' or 'kPa' 'atm' Units of the P you give

Returns

A float, rounded to decimals places, in the base unit of the solved variable:

solve_for Formula used Result unit 'P' \(P = nRT / V\) atm 'V' \(V = nRT / P\) L 'n' \(n = PV / RT\) mol 'T' \(T = PV / nR\) K

Raises

ValueError when:

  • solve_for is not one of 'P', 'V', 'n', 'T'
  • a unit option is not one of the allowed values
  • one of the three needed values is missing
  • m is given without substance
  • substance cannot be read as a formula

docs.title: Solve for pressure
docs.text:
What pressure do 4 mol of gas exert in a 5 L container at 300 K?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', V=5, n=4, T=300)
19.7

docs.title: Solve for volume
docs.text:
What volume does 1 mol of gas occupy at 273.15 K and 1 atm?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1)
22.43

docs.title: Solve for moles
docs.text:
How many moles of gas are in a 10 L tank at 2.5 atm and 298 K?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=2.5, V=10, T=298)
1.02

docs.title: Solve for temperature
docs.text:
At what temperature does 0.5 mol of gas occupy 12 L at 1 atm?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', P=1, V=12, n=0.5)
292.33

docs.title: Give a mass in place of moles
docs.text:
If you know the mass of the gas, pass it as m and name the gas with substance. The moles are worked out from the molar mass.

What volume do 10.2 g of water vapor occupy at 1.5 atm and 300 K?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', substance='H2O', m=10.2, P=1.5, T=300)
9.29

What pressure do 64 g of O₂ exert in a 10 L tank at 298 K?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', substance='O2', m=64, V=10, T=298)
4.89

If you give both n and m, n is used and m is ignored.

docs.title: Use other units for the inputs
docs.text:
Punits, Vunits and Tunits describe the values you pass in. They are converted before the equation is solved.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=740, Punits='torr', V=250, Vunits='mL', T=22, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
0.01
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=2, P=101.325, Punits='kPa', T=0, Tunits='C')
44.85
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=2, P=760, Punits='mmHg', T=0, Tunits='C')
44.85

The answer is always in atm, L, mol or K

A unit option applies only to an input. When you solve for pressure, the result is in atm whatever Punits says, because there is no pressure input to describe. Convert the result yourself:

>>> p = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', n=2, V=10, T=300)
>>> p
4.93
>>> round(p * 760, 1)
3746.8
>>> round(p * 101.325, 1)
499.5

Likewise, a temperature answer is in kelvin. Subtract 273.15 for Celsius.

>>> round(ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', P=1, V=12, n=0.5) - 273.15, 2)
19.18
Option Value Conversion applied Punits 'atm' none 'torr' or 'mmHg' divide by 760 'kPa' divide by 101.325 Vunits 'L' none 'mL' divide by 1000 Tunits 'K' none 'C' add 273.15

docs.title: Choose the number of decimals
docs.text:
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1, decimals=4)
22.4256
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1, decimals=1)
22.4

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A missing value:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', V=5, T=300)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Missing value(s) for: n

A mass without a substance:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', m=64, V=10, T=298)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: substance is required when giving the mass m

An unknown variable or unit:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('X', P=1, V=1, T=300)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: solve_for must be 'P', 'V', 'n' or 'T', not 'X'
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=1, Punits='bar', V=1, T=300)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Punits must be one of ['atm', 'kPa', 'mmHg', 'torr']

docs.title: ideal_gas_steps
docs.text:
ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps(solve_for, substance=None, P=None, V=None, n=None, T=None,
                          m=None, decimals=2, Tunits='K', Vunits='L', Punits='atm')

Prints the worked solution. It takes exactly the same arguments as ideal_gas.

Prints

  1. Any conversions needed first: mass to moles, then pressure, volume and temperature into atm, L and K.
  2. The ideal gas law.
  3. The law rearranged for the variable being solved.
  4. The values substituted in, with units, and the answer.

Examples

A direct calculation:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('P', V=5, n=4, T=300)
PV = nRT
P = nRT/V
P = 4 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 300 K / 5 L = 19.7 atm

Starting from a mass:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('V', substance='H2O', m=10.2, P=1.5, T=300)
n = 10.2g x 1 mole H2O/18.02g H2O = 0.566038 moles H2O
PV = nRT
V = nRT/P
V = 0.566038 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 300 K / 1.5 atm = 9.29 L

With unit conversions:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('n', P=740, Punits='torr', V=250, Vunits='mL', T=22, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
P = 740 torr = 0.973684 atm
V = 250 mL x 1 L/1000 mL = 0.25 L
T = (22 + 273.15) K = 295.15 K
PV = nRT
n = PV/RT
n = (0.973684 atm x 0.25 L) / (0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 295.15 K) = 0.01 moles

Solving for temperature:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('T', P=1, V=12, n=0.5)
PV = nRT
T = PV/nR
T = (1 atm x 12 L) / (0.5 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K)) = 292.33 K

Everything at once:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('P', substance='O2', m=32, V=500, Vunits='mL', T=25, Tunits='C')
n = 32g x 1 mole O2/32.0g O2 = 1 moles O2
V = 500 mL x 1 L/1000 mL = 0.5 L
T = (25 + 273.15) K = 298.15 K
PV = nRT
P = nRT/V
P = 1 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 298.15 K / 0.5 L = 48.96 atm

Numbers in the printed steps

Intermediate values in the printed solution are shown to about six significant figures. The calculation itself carries full precision, so the final answer matches ideal_gas exactly.

docs.title: The gas constant
docs.text:
>>> ideal_gas.R
0.0821

R is 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K), the value used in most general chemistry courses. It has three significant figures, so answers are good to about three significant figures. This is why the molar volume at 0 °C and 1 atm comes out as 22.43 L here, where a more precise R gives 22.41 L.

docs.title: Getting a mass as the answer
docs.text:
ideal_gas cannot solve for mass directly. Solve for moles, keeping extra decimals, then convert:

>>> from chemhelper import conversions
>>> n = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=1, V=5, T=298, decimals=4)
>>> n
0.2044
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(n, 'CO2')
9.0

docs.title: When the ideal gas law applies
docs.text: The ideal gas law assumes gas particles have no volume and do not attract one another. It works well for most gases near room temperature and atmospheric pressure. It becomes inaccurate at high pressure, at low temperature, and near the point where a gas condenses. chemhelper does not check for this.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
Temperature in Celsius without saying so. The law needs kelvin. Either convert first or pass Tunits='C'.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, P=1, T=25)
2.05
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, P=1, T=25, Tunits='C')
24.48

The first answer is wrong for a gas at 25 °C. It treats the temperature as 25 K.

Expecting the answer in your input units. Results are always atm, L, mol or K.

Forgetting substance with m. The mass can only become moles if the gas is named.

Writing a diatomic gas as a single atom. Oxygen gas is 'O2'. Using 'O' halves the molar mass and doubles the moles.

More worked problems are in the gas laws tutorial.

docs.title: Breaking / behavior changes
docs.text:
• ideal_gas('T', ...) now returns a number; it used to return the tuple (T, 2).
  • Celsius is converted with 273.15 (was 273.5).
  • Intermediate values are no longer rounded, so some results change slightly.
  • moles_to_grams now rounds to 2 decimals, like the other conversions.
  • composition and percent_composition list each element once, even when it appears more than once in the formula (e.g. CH3COOH).
  • Invalid input raises ValueError with a clear message instead of a KeyError or TypeError.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Bug reports, corrections to the chemistry, documentation fixes and new solvers are all welcome.

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text:
Open an issue with:

  • the code you ran,
  • what you expected,
  • what you got, including the full error message if there was one.

If chemhelper gives a wrong chemistry answer, a textbook reference for the right one helps a great deal.

docs.title: Set up for development
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/drosenman/chemhelper.git
cd chemhelper
pip install -e ".[test,docs]"

The -e flag installs the package in editable mode, so your changes take effect without reinstalling.

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:

This runs the tests in tests/ and every example in the docstrings.

docs.title: Work on the documentation
docs.text:
Preview the site locally. It reloads as you edit:

mkdocs serve

docs.title: Examples are executed, not typed
docs.text:
Every example in the docs is a fenced pycon block. You write only the input lines, the ones that start with >>>. A script runs them against the real package and fills in the output.

After adding or changing an example, or changing the code's behavior:

python tools/docs_examples.py --write

To check that every example is up to date without changing anything:

python tools/docs_examples.py

The check runs in CI, so documentation cannot drift from the code.

Each page gets one fresh Python session. An import at the top of a page is available to every block below it.

docs.title: The periodic table page
docs.text:
docs/periodic-table.md is generated from the element data. After changing elements.py, regenerate it:

python tools/make_periodic_table.py

docs.title: Add a solver
docs.text:
New solvers follow one pattern.

  1. Write the function that returns the answer. Give it a NumPy-style docstring with Parameters, Returns, Raises and Examples sections. Validate the inputs and raise ValueError with a message that says what is wrong.
  2. Write the _steps twin. It takes the same arguments, prints the solution with units, and returns nothing. Its final number must equal what the first function returns.
  3. Round only the final result. Carry full precision through intermediate steps.
  4. Add tests in tests/ for typical values, edge cases and each error.
  5. Document it: a section in the module's page under docs/guide/, a row in the tables in docs/guide/index.md and docs/getting-started/steps.md, and a line in CHANGELOG.md.

docs.title: Style
docs.text:
• Follow PEP 8. Lines up to 110 characters are fine.
  • Name arguments after the chemistry: mass, moles, volume, chemical.
  • Keep the dependencies small. The package needs only pandas.

docs.title: Send a pull request
docs.text:
1. Create a branch for your change.
  2. Make sure pytest, python tools/docs_examples.py and mkdocs build --strict all pass.
  3. Open a pull request describing what changed and why.

docs.title: Release checklist
docs.text:
For maintainers.

  1. Update the version in pyproject.toml and src/chemhelper/__init__.py.
  2. Add the release to CHANGELOG.md.
  3. Run the tests and the documentation check.

  4. Build and upload:

    python -m build
python -m twine upload dist/*

  5. Tag the release:

    git tag v1.0.0
git push origin v1.0.0

The documentation site is rebuilt and published automatically on every push to master.

docs.title: Is chemhelper still maintained?
docs.text: Yes. The package was first written in 2017 for tutoring and then sat for a while. Version 1.0 is a full overhaul, and development is active again. See the roadmap for what is being considered next.

docs.title: Who is it for?
docs.text: Tutors, teachers and students in a first-year general chemistry course, and anyone who wants a quick, checkable answer to a routine chemistry calculation.

docs.title: Can I use it to do my homework?
docs.text: It will give you answers, and the _steps functions will show the work. It is most useful for checking work you have already done and finding the step where yours differs.

docs.title: What license is it under?
docs.text: MIT. You can use it, change it and share it, including commercially.

docs.title: pip install chemhelper gave me version 0.4
docs.text:
Version 1.0 may not be on PyPI yet. Install from GitHub:

pip install git+https://github.com/drosenman/chemhelper.git

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'chemhelper'
docs.text: The package is installed for a different Python than the one you are running. In a notebook, install with %pip install chemhelper in a cell so it goes to the notebook's own Python.

docs.title: Which Python versions are supported?
docs.text: Python 3.10 and newer.

docs.title: Why does it need pandas?
docs.text: Element data and composition results are returned as pandas objects so they print as tidy tables and can be filtered and sorted.

docs.title: Why do I get Unknown element?
docs.text: A symbol in your formula is not one of the 92 elements chemhelper knows. Usually it is a capitalization problem: 'NACL' should be 'NaCl', and 'CL2' should be 'Cl2'. See Writing formulas.

docs.title: Why do I get Unexpected character?
docs.text: The formula contains something that is not a symbol, a digit, a parenthesis or a bracket. Lowercase first letters ('h2o'), dots ('CuSO4.5H2O') and charges ('Na+') all cause this.

docs.title: How do I write a hydrate?
docs.text: Put the water in parentheses: 'CuSO4(H2O)5'.

docs.title: How do I write an ion?
docs.text: Leave the charge off. The mass of the missing or extra electrons is far smaller than the rounding in the atomic masses.

docs.title: Can I use isotopes such as deuterium?
docs.text: Not out of the box. You can add your own element.

docs.title: Why are elements past uranium missing?
docs.text: The original table stopped at the naturally abundant elements. Adding the rest is on the roadmap.

docs.title: chemhelper accepted a formula that is not a real compound
docs.text: The parser checks that the symbols are real elements. It does not know which compounds exist. Use parse_formula to see how your string was read.

docs.title: My answer differs slightly from the textbook
docs.text:
Three things can cause a difference in the last digit:

  1. Atomic masses. chemhelper uses masses rounded to two decimals for most elements. Your table may use more digits or newer values.
  2. The gas constant. ideal_gas uses R = 0.0821. Books that use 0.08206 get slightly different answers.
  3. Rounding. chemhelper rounds only the final result. Working a problem by hand with rounded intermediate values gives a slightly different answer.

docs.title: My answer differs from chemhelper 0.4
docs.text: Version 1.0 fixed several bugs, and some results changed. See Migrating from 0.4.

docs.title: Why did grams_to_moles return 0.0?
docs.text: It rounds to two decimals, so anything under 0.005 mol rounds to zero. Divide by compounds.mass(...) yourself for small samples. See Units and rounding.

docs.title: Why does a result look like 0.30000000000000004?
docs.text: Functions that do not round return raw floating-point values. Wrap the call in round(..., 4).

docs.title: Why does a value print as np.float64(18.02)?
docs.text: Values taken out of a pandas Series are NumPy numbers. They behave like ordinary numbers. Wrap one in float() to print it plainly.

docs.title: Does chemhelper handle significant figures?
docs.text: No. It rounds to a fixed number of decimals. Apply significant-figure rules to the final answer yourself.

docs.title: The ideal gas answer is in the wrong units
docs.text: Punits, Vunits and Tunits describe your inputs only. Results are always in atm, L, mol or K. See the ideal gas guide.

docs.title: My gas answer is wildly off
docs.text: Check the temperature. If you passed Celsius without Tunits='C', it was treated as kelvin.

docs.title: A _steps function returned None
docs.text: That is expected. _steps functions print the solution and return nothing. Call the function without _steps to get the number.

docs.title: How do I get the solution as text?
docs.text: Capture the printed output. The Cookbook has a helper.

docs.title: Can it show steps with more decimal places?
docs.text: Not yet. The number of decimals in printed solutions is fixed, apart from the final answer of ideal_gas_steps, which follows decimals.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: chemhelper does not yet balance equations, read mole ratios from an equation, find limiting reagents automatically, handle pH or equilibrium, or do thermochemistry. Several of these are on the roadmap, and the Cookbook shows how to do some of them with the functions that exist today.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Open an issue on GitHub with the code you ran, what you expected and what you got.

docs.title: Migrating from 0.4
docs.text:
Version 1.0 keeps every function name and every argument from 0.4. Code written for 0.4 will run. Some of it will give different, more accurate results, and a few return types changed.

>>> from chemhelper import elements, compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Area 0.4 1.0 Do you need to change code? ideal_gas('T', ...) returned a tuple (T, 2) returns a number Yes, if you unpacked the tuple Celsius conversion added 273.5 adds 273.15 No; results change slightly Intermediate rounding moles and volumes rounded mid-calculation only the final result is rounded No; results change slightly moles_to_grams unrounded rounded to 2 decimals Only if you relied on extra digits Repeated elements listed twice in composition combined Only if you relied on duplicates Parentheses ignored, giving wrong masses supported No Bad input KeyError or TypeError ValueError with a clear message Yes, if you caught the old exceptions Technetium symbol stored as 'TC' 'Tc' No Python not specified 3.10 or newer Upgrade Python if needed

docs.title: ideal_gas returns a number when solving for temperature
docs.text:
In 0.4, solving for 'T' returned a two-item tuple by mistake.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', P=1, V=12, n=0.5)
292.33

If your code did T, _ = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', ...) or indexed the result with [0], remove that.

docs.title: Celsius is converted correctly
docs.text: 0.4 added 273.5 to Celsius temperatures. 1.0 adds 273.15. Any gas calculation with Tunits='C' changes by about 0.1 %.

docs.title: Intermediate values are no longer rounded
docs.text:
0.4 rounded moles to two decimals and converted volumes to two decimals before using them, which could shift the answer noticeably. A volume of 250 mL was fine, but 125 mL became 0.12 L.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=1, V=125, Vunits='mL', T=298, decimals=5)
0.00511

docs.title: decimals now works
docs.text:
The decimals argument of ideal_gas existed in 0.4 but was ignored.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1, decimals=4)
22.4256

docs.title: Parentheses and brackets are understood
docs.text:
0.4 ignored parentheses, so 'Ca(OH)2' was read as one Ca, one O and one H, and the mass was wrong. 1.0 reads groups correctly, including nested ones.

>>> compounds.mass('Ca(OH)2')
74.1
>>> compounds.mass('K4[Fe(CN)6]')
368.37

Check old results that used parentheses

If you used 0.4 with formulas containing parentheses, those molar masses were incorrect. Recalculate them.

docs.title: Repeated elements are combined
docs.text:
In 0.4, composition('CH3COOH') had two C rows, two H rows and two O rows. 1.0 has one of each.

>>> compounds.composition('CH3COOH')
C         24.020
H          4.032
O         32.000
Total:    60.050
Name: CH3COOH, dtype: float64

docs.title: moles_to_grams is rounded
docs.text:
It now rounds to two decimals, like grams_to_moles and molarity_to_grams.

>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(0.333, 'H2O')
6.0

docs.title: molarity uses unrounded moles
docs.text:
When given a mass, 0.4 rounded the moles to two decimals before dividing by the volume. 1.0 does not.

>>> round(conversions.molarity(1, mass=1.0, chemical='NaCl'), 4)
0.0171

In 0.4 this returned 0.02.

docs.title: Errors are ValueError
docs.text:
Invalid input used to surface as a KeyError from pandas or a TypeError from arithmetic on None. Now every invalid input raises ValueError with a message describing the problem.

>>> compounds.mass('Xy2')
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Unknown element 'Xy' in formula 'Xy2'
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', V=5, T=300)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Missing value(s) for: n
>>> conversions.molarity(1, mass=10)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
ValueError: Give either moles, or both mass and chemical.

If your code has except KeyError: around a chemhelper call, change it to except ValueError:.

docs.title: Element data corrections
docs.text:
• Technetium's symbol is 'Tc' (was 'TC').
  • Beryllium, Holmium and Protactinium are spelled correctly.
>>> elements.Tc
Element('Tc', 'Technetium', 43, 98)

docs.title: Printed solutions changed
docs.text:
The text printed by _steps functions was tidied. If you compared printed output against saved text, update the saved text. The main differences:

  • Multiplication is shown with x throughout.
  • Moles, volumes and molarities are shown to four significant figures. 0.4 showed two decimals, which turned small amounts into 0.00.
  • ideal_gas_steps prints converted values to six significant figures, and prints the law before the rearranged form for every variable.
  • molarity_to_grams_steps now starts with the molarity-to-moles line.

docs.title: New in 1.0
docs.text:
• compounds.parse_formula
  • Pressure in 'mmHg' and 'kPa'
  • ideal_gas.R
  • chemhelper.__version__
  • import chemhelper loads all four modules

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
The package name is unchanged:

pip install --upgrade chemhelper

The full list of changes is in the changelog.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
chemhelper is under active development. Version 1.0 put the foundations in order: a working package layout, a correct formula parser, tests, and this documentation. The plan now is to grow the range of problems it can solve.

Ideas, not promises

Everything on this page is a direction being considered. Nothing here has a release date. If one of these matters to you, say so in an issue, because interest decides the order.

docs.title: Smaller improvements
docs.text: Idea Why A decimals argument on every function Rounding to two decimals is too coarse for small samples Significant-figure handling Course answers are graded on significant figures _steps functions that can return text Makes it easier to use solutions in web pages and files Volume units ('mL') in conversions Matches what ideal_gas already offers Result units in ideal_gas Ask for the answer in torr, kPa, mL or °C directly Elements 93 to 118 Complete the periodic table More element data Group, period, electron configuration, electronegativity Hydrate notation ('CuSO4·5H2O') Write hydrates the way textbooks do A more precise gas constant option Match courses that use 0.08206 or 8.314

docs.title: New kinds of problems
docs.text:
Area What it would cover Chemical equations Parsing and balancing equations Stoichiometry Mole ratios, limiting reagent, theoretical and percent yield Empirical formulas From percent composition or from masses Dilution \(M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2\) as a function with steps More gas laws Combined gas law, partial pressures, gas density, molar mass of a gas Solutions Molality, mass percent, mole fraction Acids and bases pH, pOH, strong acid and base calculations, titration Thermochemistry \(q = mc\Delta T\), heats of reaction

Each new solver will follow the pattern the existing ones use: a function that returns the answer and a _steps twin that prints the work.

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text: chemhelper is a teaching and checking tool for general chemistry. It is not meant to become a cheminformatics library. Molecular structures, SMILES strings, quantum chemistry and reaction databases are out of scope; libraries such as RDKit serve those needs.

docs.title: Suggest something
docs.text: Open an issue describing the kind of problem you want solved, ideally with one worked example. If you would like to build it yourself, see Contributing.

docs.title: chemhelper.compounds
docs.text:
Molar mass and composition of chemical compounds.

Formulas are written the usual way, with case-sensitive symbols and optional counts: 'H2O', 'C6H12O6', 'Ca(OH)2', 'CH3COOH'. Parentheses and square brackets may be nested.

parse_formula(chemical)

Count the atoms of each element in a formula.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default chemical str

Chemical formula, e.g. 'Ca(OH)2'.

required

Returns:

Type Description OrderedDict

Element symbol -> number of atoms, in order of first appearance.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If the formula contains an unknown element, unbalanced parentheses or characters that are not part of a formula.

Examples:

>>> dict(parse_formula('Ca(OH)2'))
{'Ca': 1, 'O': 2, 'H': 2}
Source code in src/chemhelper/compounds.py 
def parse_formula(chemical):
    """Count the atoms of each element in a formula.

    Parameters
    ----------
    chemical : str
        Chemical formula, e.g. ``'Ca(OH)2'``.

    Returns
    -------
    collections.OrderedDict
        Element symbol -> number of atoms, in order of first appearance.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the formula contains an unknown element, unbalanced parentheses
        or characters that are not part of a formula.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> dict(parse_formula('Ca(OH)2'))
    {'Ca': 1, 'O': 2, 'H': 2}
    """
    stack = [OrderedDict()]
    pos = 0
    while pos < len(chemical):
        m = _TOKEN.match(chemical, pos)
        if not m:
            raise ValueError("Unexpected character {!r} in formula {!r}".format(chemical[pos], chemical))
        symbol, count, opening, closing, group_count, _ = m.groups()
        if symbol:
            if symbol not in elements.elements.index:
                raise ValueError("Unknown element {!r} in formula {!r}".format(symbol, chemical))
            stack[-1][symbol] = stack[-1].get(symbol, 0) + int(count or 1)
        elif opening:
            stack.append(OrderedDict())
        elif closing:
            if len(stack) == 1:
                raise ValueError("Unbalanced parentheses in formula {!r}".format(chemical))
            group = stack.pop()
            for sym, n in group.items():
                stack[-1][sym] = stack[-1].get(sym, 0) + n * int(group_count or 1)
        pos = m.end()
    if len(stack) != 1:
        raise ValueError("Unbalanced parentheses in formula {!r}".format(chemical))
    if not stack[0]:
        raise ValueError("Empty formula {!r}".format(chemical))
    return stack[0]

def mass_steps(chemical):
    """Print a step-by-step molar mass calculation.

    Parameters
    ----------
    chemical : str
        Chemical formula, e.g. ``'H2O'``.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> mass_steps('H2O')
    H2O
    H: 2 x 1.008 = 2.016
    O: 16.0
    <BLANKLINE>
    Mass H2O = 2.016 + 16.0 = 18.02
    """
    print(chemical)
    parts = []
    for sym, n in parse_formula(chemical).items():
        m = elements.elements[sym].mass
        if n == 1:
            print("{}: {}".format(sym, m))
            parts.append(m)
        else:
            print("{}: {} x {} = {}".format(sym, n, m, round(m * n, 4)))
            parts.append(round(m * n, 4))
    print("\nMass {} = {} = {}".format(chemical, " + ".join(str(p) for p in parts), mass(chemical)))

def percent_composition(chemical):

    Give either ``moles``, or ``mass`` together with ``chemical``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    volume : float
        Volume of solution in liters.
    mass : float, optional
        Mass of solute in grams.
    chemical : str, optional
        Chemical formula of the solute (required with ``mass``).
    moles : float, optional
        Moles of solute.

    float
        Molarity in mol/L.

    Examples
    --------

class Element:

    """Solve PV = nRT for one variable.

    Give every variable except ``solve_for``. Instead of ``n`` you may give the
    mass ``m`` together with ``substance``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    solve_for : {'P', 'V', 'n', 'T'}

    substance : str, optional
        Chemical formula of the gas; needed only with ``m``.
    P : float, optional
        Pressure, in ``Punits``.
    V : float, optional

    n : float, optional
        Amount of gas in moles.
    T : float, optional

    m : float, optional

    Vunits : {'L', 'mL'}, default 'L'

    Punits : {'atm', 'torr', 'mmHg', 'kPa'}, default 'atm'
        Units of the given ``P``.
