def ideal_gas_steps(solve_for, substance=None, P=None, V=None, n=None, T=None, m=None, decimals=2,
                    Tunits="K", Vunits="L", Punits="atm"):
    """Print a step-by-step ideal gas law solution.

    Takes the same arguments as :func:`ideal_gas`.

    Examples
    --------
    >>> ideal_gas_steps('V', n=1, T=273.15, P=1)
    PV = nRT
    V = nRT/P
    V = 1 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 273.15 K / 1 atm = 22.43 L
    """
    P, V, n, T = _prepare(solve_for, substance, P, V, n, T, m, Tunits, Vunits, Punits, show=True)
    result = round(_solve(solve_for, P, V, n, T), decimals)
    g = lambda x: "{:.6g}".format(x)  # noqa: E731
    print("PV = nRT")
    if solve_for == "P":
        print("P = nRT/V")
        print("P = {} moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x {} K / {} L = {} atm".format(g(n), g(T), g(V), result))
    elif solve_for == "V":
        print("V = nRT/P")
        print("V = {} moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x {} K / {} atm = {} L".format(g(n), g(T), g(P), result))
    elif solve_for == "n":
        print("n = PV/RT")
        print("n = ({} atm x {} L) / (0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x {} K) = {} moles".format(g(P), g(V), g(T), result))
    else:
        print("T = PV/nR")
        print("T = ({} atm x {} L) / ({} moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K)) = {} K".format(g(P), g(V), g(n), result))

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
The tutorials solve complete problems from start to finish, the way they come up in a course or a tutoring session. Each one uses several functions together and explains the chemistry along the way.

  • A tutoring session

    Check a student's work on a three-part ammonium nitrate problem and find where it went wrong.

  • Preparing solutions

    Weigh out a solute for a target concentration, check a solution's molarity, dilute a stock solution, and work a titration.

  • Gas law problems

    Molar volume, tank pressure from a mass of gas, mass from P, V and T, and identifying an unknown gas.

All three assume you have read the Quickstart. For short, copy-and-paste answers to single questions, see the Cookbook.

docs.title: Gas law problems
docs.text:
Six problems that cover the common shapes an ideal gas question takes. Each uses ideal_gas and, where the question involves a mass, a function from conversions or compounds.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds, conversions, ideal_gas

docs.title: 1. Volume at standard temperature and pressure
docs.text:
What volume do 2.50 mol of nitrogen gas occupy at 0 °C and 1 atm?

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=2.50, P=1, T=0, Tunits='C')
56.06
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('V', n=2.50, P=1, T=0, Tunits='C')
T = (0 + 273.15) K = 273.15 K
PV = nRT
V = nRT/P
V = 2.5 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 273.15 K / 1 atm = 56.06 L

The identity of the gas does not matter here. For an ideal gas, the volume depends only on the number of moles.

docs.title: 2. Pressure from a mass of gas
docs.text:
A 10.0 L tank holds 64.0 g of oxygen gas at 25 °C. What is the pressure?

The amount is given as a mass, so pass it as m and name the gas. Oxygen gas is O₂.

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', substance='O2', m=64.0, V=10.0, T=25, Tunits='C')
4.9
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('P', substance='O2', m=64.0, V=10.0, T=25, Tunits='C')
n = 64.0g x 1 mole O2/32.0g O2 = 2 moles O2
T = (25 + 273.15) K = 298.15 K
PV = nRT
P = nRT/V
P = 2 moles x 0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 298.15 K / 10 L = 4.9 atm

The answer is in atm. In kilopascals:

>>> p = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('P', substance='O2', m=64.0, V=10.0, T=25, Tunits='C')
>>> round(p * 101.325, 1)
496.5

docs.title: 3. Mass of gas from pressure, volume and temperature
docs.text:
How many grams of carbon dioxide are in a 5.00 L flask at 740 torr and 22 °C?

ideal_gas solves for moles, not mass. Solve for moles first, asking for extra decimals so the next step is not working from a rounded number:

>>> n = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=740, Punits='torr', V=5.00, T=22, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
>>> n
0.2009

Then convert moles to grams:

>>> conversions.moles_to_grams(n, 'CO2')
8.84

The two worked solutions, one after the other:

>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas_steps('n', P=740, Punits='torr', V=5.00, T=22, Tunits='C', decimals=4)
P = 740 torr = 0.973684 atm
T = (22 + 273.15) K = 295.15 K
PV = nRT
n = PV/RT
n = (0.973684 atm x 5 L) / (0.0821 L*atm/(mol*K) x 295.15 K) = 0.2009 moles
>>> conversions.moles_to_grams_steps(n, 'CO2')
CO2
C: 12.01
O: 2 x 16.0 = 32.0

Mass CO2 = 12.01 + 32.0 = 44.01
0.2009 moles x 44.01 grams/mole = 8.84 grams

docs.title: 4. Temperature
docs.text:
To what temperature must 0.500 mol of gas be heated to fill a 15.0 L container at 1.00 atm?

>>> t = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('T', P=1.00, V=15.0, n=0.500)
>>> t
365.41

The result is in kelvin. In Celsius:

>>> round(t - 273.15, 2)
92.26

docs.title: 5. Identify an unknown gas
docs.text:
1.25 g of an unknown gas occupies 1.00 L at 0 °C and 1.00 atm. Is the gas N₂, O₂ or CO₂?

Find the moles of gas from P, V and T. Then the molar mass is the mass divided by the moles.

>>> n = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=1.00, V=1.00, T=0, Tunits='C', decimals=5)
>>> n
0.04459
>>> round(1.25 / n, 1)
28.0

Compare with the candidates:

>>> {gas: compounds.mass(gas) for gas in ['N2', 'O2', 'CO2']}
{'N2': 28.02, 'O2': 32.0, 'CO2': 44.01}

The unknown gas is nitrogen.

Carbon monoxide has the same molar mass

CO would match as well:

>>> compounds.mass('CO')
28.01

A molar mass narrows the options but cannot always decide between them.

docs.title: 6. Changing conditions
docs.text:
A balloon holds 2.00 L of helium at 25 °C and 1.00 atm. What is its volume at −10 °C and 0.700 atm?

The amount of gas is constant. Find it from the first set of conditions, then use it with the second:

>>> n = ideal_gas.ideal_gas('n', P=1.00, V=2.00, T=25, Tunits='C', decimals=5)
>>> ideal_gas.ideal_gas('V', n=n, P=0.700, T=-10, Tunits='C')
2.52

This is the combined gas law, \(P_1 V_1 / T_1 = P_2 V_2 / T_2\), done by way of the moles.

docs.title: Checklist for gas problems
docs.text:
1. Decide what you are solving for. That is solve_for.
  2. List the three known quantities. If one is a mass, use m and substance.
  3. Note the units of each input and set Punits, Vunits and Tunits if they are not atm, L and K.
  4. Read the answer in atm, L, mol or K and convert if the question asks for something else.
  5. Keep extra decimals with decimals= when the result feeds another calculation.

docs.title: Preparing solutions
docs.text:
Three tasks come up again and again at the bench: making a solution of a known concentration, checking the concentration of a solution you made, and diluting a stock solution.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds, conversions

All volumes in conversions are in liters.

docs.title: Make a solution of a target concentration
docs.text:
You need 250 mL of 0.100 M sodium hydroxide. How many grams of NaOH do you weigh out?

Convert the volume to liters (0.250 L), then ask for the grams of solute:

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.100, 0.250, 'NaOH')
1.0

The worked solution shows the three steps: moles needed, the molar mass of NaOH, and the mass:

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams_steps(0.100, 0.250, 'NaOH')
0.1 moles/L x 0.25 L = 0.025 moles
NaOH
Na: 22.99
O: 16.0
H: 1.008

Mass NaOH = 22.99 + 16.0 + 1.008 = 40.0
0.025 moles x 40.00 grams/mole = 1.00 grams

So you would dissolve that mass of NaOH and add water until the total volume is 250 mL.

Fill to the mark

Molarity is moles per liter of solution. Add water up to a final volume of 250 mL. Do not add 250 mL of water to the solid.

docs.title: Check the concentration of a solution
docs.text:
You dissolved 5.85 g of NaCl and made the volume up to 500 mL. What is the molarity?

>>> conversions.molarity(0.500, mass=5.85, chemical='NaCl')
0.2002053388090349
>>> conversions.molarity_steps(0.500, mass=5.85, chemical='NaCl')
5.85g NaCl x 1 mole NaCl/58.44g NaCl = 0.1001 moles NaCl
0.1001 moles/0.5 L = 0.2002 M

molarity returns the unrounded value. Round it for reporting:

>>> round(conversions.molarity(0.500, mass=5.85, chemical='NaCl'), 3)
0.2

docs.title: How many moles are in a sample of solution?
docs.text:
How many moles of HCl are in 25.0 mL of 0.150 M hydrochloric acid?

>>> round(conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.150, 0.0250), 5)
0.00375
>>> conversions.molarity_to_moles_steps(0.150, 0.0250)
0.15 moles/L x 0.025 L = 0.00375 moles

This is the first step of most titration calculations.

docs.title: Dilute a stock solution
docs.text:
50.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl is diluted to a final volume of 400 mL. What is the new concentration?

Dilution adds water but not solute, so the moles of HCl stay the same. Find them from the stock solution, then divide by the new volume:

>>> moles = conversions.molarity_to_moles(2.00, 0.0500)
>>> moles
0.1
>>> conversions.molarity(0.400, moles=moles)
0.25

This is the same calculation as the dilution equation \(M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2\), done in two visible steps.

docs.title: How much stock do I need?
docs.text:
What volume of 12.0 M HCl is needed to make 1.00 L of 0.500 M HCl?

Work backwards: find the moles the final solution must contain, then the volume of stock that holds that many moles.

>>> moles_needed = conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.500, 1.00)
>>> moles_needed
0.5
>>> liters_of_stock = moles_needed / 12.0
>>> round(liters_of_stock * 1000, 1)
41.7

That is the volume of concentrated acid, in milliliters, to dilute to 1.00 L.

docs.title: A titration, start to finish
docs.text:
25.0 mL of sulfuric acid is neutralized by 32.4 mL of 0.100 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

H₂SO₄ + 2 NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2 H₂O

Moles of base used:

>>> moles_naoh = conversions.molarity_to_moles(0.100, 0.0324)
>>> round(moles_naoh, 5)
0.00324

The balanced equation says one mole of acid reacts with two moles of base. chemhelper does not read equations, so apply that ratio yourself:

>>> moles_h2so4 = moles_naoh / 2

Concentration of the acid:

>>> round(conversions.molarity(0.0250, moles=moles_h2so4), 4)
0.0648

docs.title: Mass of solute in a bottle
docs.text:
A 2.00 L bottle is labeled 0.250 M glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆. How many grams of glucose does it contain?

>>> conversions.molarity_to_grams(0.250, 2.00, 'C6H12O6')
90.08

docs.title: A tutoring session
docs.text:
chemhelper was written for this situation: a student brings you a problem and their attempt at it. You want to know quickly whether each answer is right, and if not, exactly where the work went off course.

>>> from chemhelper import compounds, conversions

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃, is a common fertilizer.

  1. What is the percent by mass of nitrogen in ammonium nitrate?
  2. How many moles are in a 25.0 g sample?
  3. If that sample is dissolved in enough water to make 500 mL of solution, what is the molarity?

The student's answers are 17.5 %, 0.31 mol and 0.62 M.

docs.title: Part 1: percent nitrogen
docs.text:
Check the answer first.

>>> compounds.percent_composition('NH4NO3')
N          35.002
H           5.037
O          59.961
Total:    100.000
Name: NH4NO3, dtype: float64

The student said 17.5 %, which is half of the correct value. That is a strong hint. Print the solution to see the structure of the calculation:

>>> compounds.percent_composition_steps('NH4NO3')
NH4NO3
N: 2 x 14.01 = 28.02
H: 4 x 1.008 = 4.032
O: 3 x 16.0 = 48.0

Mass NH4NO3 = 28.02 + 4.032 + 48.0 = 80.05

N         28.020
H          4.032
O         48.000
Total:    80.050
Name: NH4NO3, dtype: float64
N: 100 x 28.02g N/80.05g NH4NO3 = 35.00%
H: 100 x 4.032g H/80.05g NH4NO3 = 5.04%
O: 100 x 48.0g O/80.05g NH4NO3 = 59.96%

The first lines show it: nitrogen appears twice in NH₄NO₃, once in the ammonium ion and once in the nitrate ion, so its contribution is 2 × 14.01. The student counted one nitrogen.

You can confirm how the formula is read:

>>> dict(compounds.parse_formula('NH4NO3'))
{'N': 2, 'H': 4, 'O': 3}

Teaching point

Ask the student to count the atoms of each element before doing any arithmetic. parse_formula gives you the count to compare against.

docs.title: Part 2: grams to moles
docs.text:
>>> conversions.grams_to_moles(25.0, 'NH4NO3')
0.31

The student's 0.31 mol is correct. If they want to see it laid out anyway:

>>> conversions.grams_to_moles_steps(25.0, 'NH4NO3')
25.0g NH4NO3 x 1 mole NH4NO3/80.05g NH4NO3 = 0.31 moles NH4NO3

Notice that the molar mass in this step was right, even though part 1 was wrong. The student can find a molar mass. The slip in part 1 was specific to picking out nitrogen's share of it.

docs.title: Part 3: molarity
docs.text:
The volume must be in liters: 500 mL is 0.500 L.

>>> conversions.molarity(0.500, mass=25.0, chemical='NH4NO3')
0.6246096189881324
>>> conversions.molarity_steps(0.500, mass=25.0, chemical='NH4NO3')
25.0g NH4NO3 x 1 mole NH4NO3/80.05g NH4NO3 = 0.3123 moles NH4NO3
0.3123 moles/0.5 L = 0.6246 M

The student's 0.62 M matches.

Why 0.31 mol in part 2 but 0.3123 mol here

grams_to_moles rounds its answer to two decimals. molarity carries the unrounded moles through to the end, and its printed solution shows four significant figures. See Units and rounding.

docs.title: What the session looked like
docs.text:
Part Student Verdict 1. Percent N 17.5 % Wrong: counted one N, not two 2. Moles 0.31 mol Correct 3. Molarity 0.62 M Correct

Three checks and one diagnosis took a handful of lines. The rest of the session can go to the idea the student actually needs: reading a formula that contains the same element in two places.

docs.title: The pattern
docs.text:
1. Check with the plain function.
  2. If the answer is wrong, print the solution with the _steps twin.
  3. Compare line by line with the student's work to find the first difference.
  4. Use parse_formula when the disagreement starts at the formula itself.
